answer: The first century in which Diversity in Pottery Decoration and Diversity in Pottery Form show opposite growth trends — Pottery Decoration increasing significantly while Pottery Form declines — is the 18th century BCE (the 1800–1700 BC interval, marking the transition into the 17th century BCE). Over that century the Pottery Form Z-value fell from +0.74 to −1.13 (Δ = −1.87) while the Pottery Decoration Z-value rose from −0.48 to +0.97 (Δ = +1.45), each move being ≈ 3.9–4.0 standard deviations of the pre-1800 BCE century-to-century change variability. Every earlier century (4300→1800 BCE) had the two series moving in the same direction or flat, so no earlier century qualifies at any magnitude.

payload.hypothesis: The first century of opposite growth — Pottery Decoration increasing significantly while Pottery Form declines — is the 18th century BCE (1800–1700 BC, transition into the 17th century BCE): Pottery Form Δ=−1.87 (0.74→−1.13) and Pottery Decoration Δ=+1.45 (−0.48→+0.97), each ≈4 SD of pre-transition century-change variability; all earlier centuries (4300→1800 BCE) moved together or flat.
payload.workflow: Load data/capital.csv (primary; ZKeform=Pottery Form, Zkeverz=Pottery Decoration; parse European comma decimals), verify against data/time_series_data.csv anchors (PotteryForm/PotteryDecoration; 37/37 exact matches); sort BCE descending (oldest→most recent); compute per-century Δ over successive 100-yr anchors; flag first bin with sign(ΔForm)<0 AND sign(ΔDec)>0; assess significance vs pre-transition century-change distribution (≈4 SD); pollen file held as context only (no pottery variables).
